messages.subject: How to calculate in how many SSR repeats MLGs differ between each other?
messages.subject_clean: How to calculate in how many SSR repeats MLGs differ between each other?
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I have SSR data on 400 B. cinerea isolates that were collected from flowers, as well as green and ripe fruit from 40 raspberry inflorescences. The isolates from flowers/fruit are grouped by cluster. The genotypic diversity of the isolates is pretty high (almost every isolate is represented by a different MLG). However, from row data I can see that some MLGs differ between each other by only one microsatellite repeat, some - by two, others - by three etc.

One of the questions that I want to answer is : are the isolates from flowers more closely related to each other than isolates from fruit, or flower and fruit?

The MSN gives me distance between haplotypes in Bruvo distance as a gray scale, but I additionally would like to know in how many repeats the isolates differ between each other. Is there a way to get this information from MSN or Poppr in general?

Thank you very much for the advice

Olga

messages.subject_clean: [poppr] Error with bootstrapping NJ trees - "Error in dimnames(x)"
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

The problem here is that somehow, the loc.names slot and the column names in the genind object don't match up. This is caused by having "." in the locus names. I suspect it's a problem with df2genind() (which read.genalex calls), but I'm not exactly sure. I'll have a look into that and try to fix the problem for the next versions.

In the mean time, a fix for you is to read in your genalex file, replace the "." with "_", and then use df2genind() to import it like so:

collected.df <- read.csv("DataBinaryT-seasons-justV.csv",
                         skip = 2,
                         header = TRUE,
                         check.names = FALSE)
colnames(collected.df) <- gsub("[.]", "_", colnames(collected.df))
collected <- df2genind(collected.df[, -c(1:2)],
          ind.names = collected.df[[1]],
          strata = data.frame(pop = collected.df[[2]]),
          type = "PA",
          ncode = 1L)
collected <- as.genclone(collected)

After that, the bootstrapping function should work.

Best,
Zhian

messages.body_plain:
Hi Olga,

If you specify `by_locus = TRUE` in Bruvo's distance, you will get a list of distances, one element per locus (see the documentation: https://grunwaldlab.github.io/poppr/reference/bruvo.dist.html).
Because you have a haploid organism, you can back-calculate from this result to find out how many repeats you have per locus by using -log(1 - i, 2) like so:

res <- bruvo.dist(..., by_locus = TRUE)
n_repeats <- function(i) -log(1 - i, 2)
lapply(res, n_repeats)

Hope that helps,
Zhian

Hi Zhian,

I'm running an AMOVA, and I'm unsure whether to trust these results. Although the high variance within individuals is interesting here, it doesn't seem biologically plausible... however, I'm more concerned about the magnitude of the negative variance (sigma) observed between populations (see attached).

Would it be correct to assume that poppr is controlling for within-individual and between-sample variance when testing for between-population variance, and that's why poppr finds no evidence of population structure? AMOVAs in pegas and adonis show significant population structure, but neither is testing for within-population variance. Regardless, "population" doesn't seem to matter much: in adonis and pegas, population explains only ~9% of the variance, and in poppr, it explains -0.26% of the variance.

For background, my data come from sexually reproducing populations (n=158) with 3,000+ SNPs going into the genetic distance matrix. I find exceptionally low FST among "populations," no clear structure based on PCA, STRUCTURE, DAPC, etc.

Thanks for any insight you can provide!
Natalie

There can be a number of reason why you are seeing negative variance. The best explanation I've seen is from Excoffier (http://cmpg.unibe.ch/software/arlequin/software/2.000/doc/faq/faqlist.htm):
>
> > Negative variance components can sometimes occur, because they are rather covariances. Their associated fixation indices can also be seen as correlation coefficients. Usually, slightly negative variance components can occur in absence of genetic structure, because the true value of the parameter you want to estimate is zero. Thus, if the expectation of the estimator is zero, you can have, by chance, slightly positive or slightly negative variance components. Most of the time, these negative variance components indicate an absence of genetic structure. They can have a biological meaning, though. For instance, in outcrossing organisms, genes from different populations can be more related to each other than genes from the same population.
>
> That being said, you need to consider whether or not assessing within-individual variance makes sense in this context.
>
> Again, I hope that helps.

Hi Natalie,

My first recommendation would be to run AMOVA again with the option: method = "pegas" just to make sure that what you are seeing is not a bug in the ade4 version. I think, here, however, Excoffier's explanation for negative variance still applies.

strata(nancycats) <- data.frame(pop = pop(nancycats))
set.seed(2018-07-18)
nan <- nancycats[pop = sample(nPop(nancycats), 5)]
poppr.amova(shufflepop(nan), ~pop)$componentsofcovariance

I've written a small example of how to choose a cutoff threshold here: https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/poppr/vignettes/mlg.html#choosing-a-threshold. For comparisons between the performance of microsatellite markers and SNP markers to detect clonal lineages, see Rafiei et al. 2017: https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/ppa.12713

Additionally, if things are moving a bit slow or taking up a lot of memory on your machine, you may want to consider using the snpclone/genlight object to store your data in your R session; it's 8 times more memory efficient with the caveat that it assumes biallelic SNPs. If your data are in PLINK or VCF format, then there is the adegenet::read.PLINK() and vcfR::read.vcfR()/vcfR::vcfR2genlight() functions.

Hope that helps!
Zhian

Hello,

While there is no one function from poppr that can do this analysis, R is versatile enough to allow you to write one to perform this procedure. Here are the steps:

1. create a 3D, NxNx100 array like so: A <- array(data = 0, dim = c(nPop(myData), nPop(myData), 100)))

Now, in a loop:
2. sample one individual from each population
3. calculate Bruvo's distance and convert to a matrix
4. place that matrix into the 3rd index of the array like so: A[, , i] <- theDistance

Once the loop is finished, use the apply function to calculate the mean and standard deviation across cells:

apply(A, MARGIN = 1:2, FUN = mean, na.rm = TRUE)
apply(A, MARGIN = 1:2, FUN = sd, na.rm = TRUE)

Hope that helps,
Zhian

Hi Max,

> Would you say that my analysis makes sense?

I'd say that what you've presented so far makes sense.

> Choosing the threshold by eye, I would say there is a steep increase for genetic distances < 0.001 (red vertical line), for a total of 151 unique genotypes. When using cutoff_predictor, the threshold is 0.0122 (blue line), which visually does not seem very intuitive, although the result is almost identical (149 unique genotypes).

cutoff_predictor() is kind of ham-fisted. All it wants to do is to find the largest gap between points on the left side of the plot and draw a line down the middle of it. That being said, it does work pretty well. The rationale behind it is that you set the threshold high enough to retain all the possible mutations encountered in a multilocus lineage but low enough that you don't drag in sister clades. Additionally, the problem with choosing a threshold by eye from the histogram is that histograms are also ham-fisted ways of representing data, so the analysis by eye may be different with a different representation of the data ¯\_(ツ)_/¯.

Of course, this all gets into the question of "What is a clone, anyways?", and your choice of threshold ultimately depends on that definition and how much stock you put into your markers.

But, I digress; your analysis thusfar seems perfectly fine to me!

Cheers,
Zhian
